abstract: The Rise of the Network Society is the first volume of Manuel Castells' trilogy The Information Age: Economy, Society, and Culture, presented here in its second edition with a substantial new preface written for the 2010 reissue. Drawing on multi-continental research, Castells develops a systematic theory of a new social structure — the network society — arising from the interaction of the information technology revolution, capitalist restructuring, and social movements from the late twentieth century onward. The new preface revisits the book's core hypotheses in light of the 2008 global financial crisis, the transformation of work and communication, the diffusion of the Internet and mobile telephony, and the accelerating global urbanization into polycentric metropolitan regions.
key_claims: A new social structure, the network society, has emerged globally, organized around digital networks that operate across all key domains of social organization.

Informationalism, understood as a distinct mode of development based on knowledge and information processing, has combined with restructured capitalism to produce a new economy characterized by productivity growth, globalization, and networking.
The global economy operates as a 'global automaton' of interdependent financial markets that has escaped effective regulation by nation-states, as demonstrated by the 2008 financial crisis.
Work has been restructured into a polarized structure of 'self-programmable labor' and 'generic labor,' generating rising inequality alongside overall skill upgrading.
Communication has been transformed by the rise of 'mass self-communication' via the Internet, wireless devices, and Web 2.0 platforms, producing a culture of 'real virtuality.'

Space and time in the network society are reorganized around a 'space of flows' and 'timeless time,' with polycentric metropolitan regions replacing traditional city forms as the dominant spatial pattern.
Nation-states have been both agents and victims of globalization, losing regulatory capacity over global flows of capital, information, and communication.
methods: Comparative, multi-regional empirical research drawing on studies in the USA, Asia, Latin America, and Europe.
Synthesis of secondary data on productivity, trade, foreign direct investment, employment, occupational structure, and demographics (G-7 countries, 1920–2005).
Case studies of technological milieus (e.g., Silicon Valley), East Asian business networks (Japan, Korea, China), and firms such as Cisco.
Analysis of statistical indicators on Internet and mobile-phone diffusion, media consumption, migration, and urbanization.
Theoretical construction of new conceptual categories (network society, space of flows, timeless time, real virtuality, network enterprise, mass self-communication) to interpret assembled evidence.
Grounded, non-predictive social-scientific interpretation, explicitly disavowing futurology.
findings: Digital networking technologies allowed networked forms of organization to overcome traditional size and complexity limits, enabling globalization on a new scale.
US cumulative productivity grew nearly 30% between 1998 and 2008, while real wages stagnated and financial-sector profits rose from 10% to 40% of all profits, fueling the credit and housing bubble.
Household debt as a share of disposable income in the US grew from 3% (1998) to 130% (2008), and prime mortgage delinquencies rose from 2.5% to 118% of loans.
Global Internet users grew from under 40 million in 1995 to about 1.5 billion in 2009, while wireless subscriptions grew from ~16 million in 1991 to over 3.4 billion by mid-2008.
The digital divide (OECD vs. developing countries) narrowed from 80.6:1 in 1997 to 5.8:1 in 2007; China surpassed the US in absolute Internet users by 2008.
Immigration involves roughly 250 million people worldwide but is concentrated in metropolitan cores, exaggerating its perceived pervasiveness.

Over half of the world's population is now urban, with polycentric metropolitan regions (e.g., the Pearl River Delta region of ~60 million people; Southern California) emerging as the dominant spatial form.
Labor markets have polarized between highly educated 'self-programmable' workers and 'generic' executants, with growing use of part-time, temporary, and self-employed arrangements.

Traditional mass media are converging with Internet-based horizontal communication networks, giving rise to user-generated platforms (YouTube, MySpace, Facebook, Wikipedia, Second Life, MMOGs like World of Warcraft).
contributions: Provides a foundational theoretical vocabulary — network society, space of flows, timeless time, informationalism, network enterprise, real virtuality, mass self-communication — that has become widely used in sociology, geography, and communication studies.
Offers an integrated, empirically grounded account of how technology, economy, culture, and space have been co-transformed in the late twentieth and early twenty-first centuries.
Introduces a distinction between modes of production (capitalism/statism) and modes of development (industrialism/informationalism), refining classical macro-sociological categories.
Reframes globalization as a networked, selective process that includes some territories and populations while excluding others.
The 2010 preface offers a retrospective assessment linking the trilogy's original analyses to the 2008 financial crisis, the mobile Internet era, and contemporary urbanization patterns.
Advances a network-based theory of urbanism grounded in comparative research on global cities and polycentric metropolitan regions.
framing: The book positions itself as a major sociological synthesis charting the transition from industrial to informational society, in dialogue with theorists such as Giddens, and with urban and economic geographers including Saskia Sassen, Peter Hall, Peter Taylor, Michael Dear, Anna Lee Saxenian, and Doreen Massey. It combines Weberian and post-Marxian macro-sociology with the sociology of technology and communication, seeking to provide new intellectual categories adequate to a historical transformation that older industrial-era frameworks cannot grasp.
